extracted.intended_audience: industrial employers, factory managers, and philanthropists
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance—drawn from Carnegie's memoir—on managing labor relations in heavy industry (contracts, negotiations, wage systems, welfare measures) and on principles for distributing large private wealth (relief funds, libraries, research institutions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect and enforce written agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not yield to demands that require breaking an existing agreement; signed agreements should be carried out and treated as binding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie recounts refusing to yield to a committee that threatened to leave before the contract expired: 'The worst day that labor has ever seen in this world is that day in which it dishonors itself by breaking its agreement.' If a worker signed carelessly, the best way is to carry out the provisions and be more careful next time. Example: confronting a chairman who had signed without reading and urging continuation under the existing agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat workers with courtesy and sincere interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Receive committees and workmen with courtesy and genuine interest—this builds loyalty and prevents quarrels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie stresses that courteous treatment is not merely good policy but sincere enjoyment of meeting men; he attributes many prevented disputes to fair treatment and appreciation. Example: treating committees 'with great courtesy' and enjoying conferences not always about wages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a sliding wage scale tied to product prices
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt wages on a sliding scale based on the price of the product so capital and labor share prosperity and adversity; include a minimum to guarantee living wages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sliding scale 'makes capital and labor partners' and should have a minimum. Carnegie implemented a three-year sliding scale (later recommending no fixed end date but notice periods). It enables the company to meet markets and helps keep works running, which benefits workers through steadier employment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid fixed short-term scales; prefer open scales with notice
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not set yearly scales that invite struggle; better to set no date for ending a scale and require six months' or a year's notice on either side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie criticizes yearly scales as provoking preparations for conflict; advising longer or indefinite terms with formal notice reduces incentives to fight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require worker-level assent in addition to union officer signatures
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow union officers to sign agreements but require every workman to sign also so individuals explicitly consent and unions cannot bind men unilaterally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie allowed union officers to sign, then asked each man to sign too; this made it impossible for the union alone to bind men for long terms and undermined the union's ability to claim it could act for them—eventually the union was deserted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insist on clear democratic procedures for major actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Major operational changes (e.g., restarting mills) should be subject to clear vote thresholds (Carnegie required a two-thirds majority to restart).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie told men that 'these works will never start except upon a sliding scale based upon the prices we get' and later that works 'will never start until the men vote by a two-thirds majority to start them', using governance rules to stabilize outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use firm but nonviolent resolve in disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not seek to 'fight' labor violently; be prepared to stand firm and outlast coercive tactics while avoiding physical confrontation when possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie emphasizes he would not fight labor physically but would 'beat any committee that was ever made at sitting down'—i.e., strategic firmness (e.g., refusing to restart works until conditions met) rather than violent suppression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appoint managers who genuinely like and respect workmen
rubrics_metrics.description: Place in charge those managers who have authentic goodwill toward employees; such managers restore order and maintain harmony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie credits returning 'Charlie' Schwab to Homestead with restoring peace because 'Charlie liked his workmen and they liked him'; implies manager selection is crucial to industrial peace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use conciliatory social methods to build rapport before negotiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Build relationships by socializing and avoiding immediate hard bargaining; delay formal negotiation until proper internal votes are taken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: hosting visiting committee members, showing them New York and taking them to lunch, purposely avoiding discussions of the dispute until they had voted—this helped calm tensions and led to agreement later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide practical welfare measures that cost little but help greatly
rubrics_metrics.description: Implement low-cost concessions (e.g., biweekly pay, coöperative store, coal at net cost, delivered coal) that materially improve workers' lives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific measures Carnegie adopted: paying men every two weeks (equivalent to a 10% raise for careful men), helping found a cooperative store (company paid rent but men managed stock), selling coal at net cost and arranging delivery—each had big morale and economic benefits for workers at small employer cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer employee savings and home-loan trust funds
rubrics_metrics.description: Accept and safeguard workers' savings (separate from business), pay interest (Carnegie paid 6% up to $2,000), and lend to workers for home building.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie describes the trust fund as encouraging thrift, keeping money separate from business, and enabling loans for homes—one of his best services to labor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create relief funds and small pensions for accidents and old age
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish formal relief funds to relieve those suffering accidents and provide small pensions to those needing help in old age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On retiring Carnegie dedicated bonds to an 'Andrew Carnegie Relief Fund' 'designed to relieve those who may suffer from accidents, and provide small pensions for those needing help in old age.' Such funds were publicly appreciated by employees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinstate nonviolent workers and favor reconciliation after disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: After unrest, dismiss suits and reinstate old men not guilty of violence; favor reconciliation rather than permanent punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie recounts promptly dismissing suits against many strikers and taking back all old men who had not been guilty of violence—practices that helped restore harmony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shorten working hours toward an eight-hour day
rubrics_metrics.description: Work toward reducing labor hours; Carnegie predicts 'Eight hours will be the rule—eight for work, eight for sleep, and eight for rest and recreation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a progressive goal accompanying industrial development and improved worker welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Go beyond contractual obligations—employer generosity returns dividends
rubrics_metrics.description: Exceed the letter of contractual obligations in favor of workers; such expenditures repay themselves via loyalty and fewer disputes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie asserts 'No expenditure returned such dividends as the friendship of our workmen' and regrets not having been even more generous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philanthropic principle: wise distribution of surplus wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon retiring from business, cease accumulating and undertake the task of wise distribution—support public institutions such as libraries, schools, research organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie describes giving bonds to relief funds, libraries, the Carnegie Institution, and the Carnegie Institute at Pittsburgh. He frames philanthropy as encouraging 'investigations, research and discovery, and the application of knowledge to the improvement of mankind' and advises cooperation with governments, universities, and learned societies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endow research with the explicit mission to advance knowledge and application
rubrics_metrics.description: Foundations/institutions should be established 'to encourage in the broadest and most liberal manner investigations, research and discovery, and the application of knowledge to the improvement of mankind.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie quotes the incorporation language of the Carnegie Institution, specifying cooperation with governments, universities, colleges, technical schools, learned societies, and individuals—suggesting philanthropic endowments should have clear public-minded research missions and institutional partnerships.
